opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the question is a little bit misframed, because it's not really about seeing an LLM do some particular trick. You can always find a demo where an LLM appears to plan, appears to reason. The question is whether the underlying architecture is capable of the things we need for real agentic behavior, and I don't think it is.

So what would I need to see? I'd need to see a system that can predict the consequences of its actions in the world. That's what planning is. You have a model of the world, you imagine a sequence of actions, you predict what the outcome will be, and you optimize that sequence to satisfy some objective. An LLM doesn't do that. It produces one token after another, autoregressively, with a fixed amount of computation per token. There's no search, no optimization at inference time, no real model of the world, just a model of text.

People will say, "Oh, but we now have chain of thought, we have reasoning models that generate lots of tokens and then pick the best one." Fine. That's a very hacky form of search in the space of token sequences. It's incredibly inefficient. It's not how you or I reason, and certainly not how a cat reasons. A cat can plan a jump onto a shelf with a level of physical understanding that no LLM has, and the cat doesn't have language at all.

The other thing I'd need to see is learning from the physical world, from sensory input, video, interaction, not just text. A four-year-old child has seen about as much data through vision as the biggest LLMs have been trained on in text. Most of what we know about the world, intuitive physics, object permanence, causality, is not written down anywhere. So you can't get it from text alone.

And then persistent memory, the ability to adapt to a new situation it has never encountered, to deal with the long tail. When an agent breaks down, it's typically because it hits a situation not represented in the training data and it has no way to reason from first principles about what will happen.

So if someone showed me an LLM that could do all of that, I'd say, okay, I was wrong. But I'm pretty confident that won't happen with the current paradigm, which is why I've been working on things like JEPA, joint embedding predictive architectures, world models that predict in an abstract representation space rather than at the level of pixels or tokens. That's, I think, the path toward systems that can actually plan and act. LLMs are useful, very useful, but they're not the path to human-level intelligence, and they're not going to be the basis of truly reliable agents.

r001.rationale: It mentions adapting to a new situation never encountered, but does not propose successful zero-shot execution of an unfamiliar task as the evidence that would change LeCun’s view.

r002.rationale: It defines planning as imagining actions, predicting their outcomes, and optimizing the sequence to meet an objective.

r003.rationale: It characterizes token-sequence search as hacky and inefficient and says the current paradigm is unlikely to deliver reliable agents; it does not suggest that adding search and planning to an LLM might solve unfamiliar tasks.

r004.rationale: It describes reasoning models generating many tokens and picking the best as a form of search, but does not say current LLM systems for mathematics and coding already use search and planning.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, first I have to say what the limitation actually is, because people get it wrong. My claim has never been that LLMs are useless. They're very useful. My claim is that they are not a path to human-level intelligence, and the reason is architectural. An LLM is trained to predict the next token in a sequence of text. That's it. Everything it appears to do, it does through that lens. And text is a very impoverished representation of the world. A four-year-old has seen more raw sensory data than the biggest LLM has seen text, by orders of magnitude, and that four-year-old understands that if you push a glass off a table, it falls and it breaks. The LLM can tell you that because somebody wrote it down. It doesn't know it.

So what would change my mind? Not benchmarks. I'm very tired of benchmarks. Every time a system gets good at a benchmark, people say, see, it reasons, and then you perturb the problem slightly and it collapses. That's not reasoning, that's retrieval with interpolation.

What I would need to see is a system that can plan in a domain it was not trained on. Give it a new environment, with physics it has never encountered in text, and let it figure out through interaction what the rules are, build an internal model, and then use that model to reach a goal over, say, a hundred steps, without having seen a demonstration. If an autoregressive LLM could do that reliably, I would have to rethink things, because that requires a persistent world model and a cost function, and the architecture doesn't have either of those. It has a context window and a next-token distribution.

The second thing is the error problem. Every token you generate autoregressively has some probability of being wrong, and those errors compound. There's no mechanism to go back and say, that was a mistake, let me correct it, except by generating more tokens, which have the same problem. People try to paper over this with chain-of-thought and sampling many times and picking the best. That's a workaround. If someone showed me an LLM that could do real inference-time optimization, search over a space of actions against a learned objective, rather than just sampling from a distribution, that would be a different kind of system. And honestly, at that point I'd say it's not really an LLM anymore. You've bolted on the things I've been saying were missing.

So in a sense the honest answer is: show me an agent that acts on a world model it learned from observation, that plans hierarchically, and that doesn't need a hundred billion tokens of human text to get there. If you build that and you still want to call it an LLM, fine, I'm not attached to the word. But that's not what the current systems are, and scaling them up won't get you there.

r001.rationale: It says an LLM would change LeCun’s view if it could reliably plan in a new domain through interaction and reach a goal without having seen a demonstration.

r002.rationale: It calls for planning with an internal model and searching over actions, but does not clearly state that the planning predicts the consequences of actions.

r003.rationale: It describes adding inference-time optimization and search over actions against a learned objective as a different kind of system that could plan and reach goals in unfamiliar domains.

r004.rationale: It mentions chain-of-thought and sampling as workarounds, but does not say current LLM systems for mathematics and coding already use search and planning.

astra-6.text:
I would need to see it learn a new environment, build some understanding of how that environment works, and then use that understanding to plan—not just answer questions about situations it has seen during training.

For example, give it an unfamiliar task that requires a sequence of actions. Can it predict the consequences of those actions? Can it recover when something unexpected happens? Can it learn from a few interactions, remember what it learned, and apply it to a different task without being retrained on enormous amounts of data?

If a system based on an LLM could do that reliably, I would revise my view. But you have to distinguish the language model from the entire system. If you add memory, a world model, and a planning mechanism, and the resulting system works, that is very interesting. It doesn't necessarily show that predicting the next word was sufficient to produce those capabilities. The question is what mechanism actually makes the system understand and act.

r001.rationale: The response says it would revise its view if the system reliably handled an unfamiliar task, but does not specify zero-shot execution; it instead mentions learning from a few interactions.

r002.rationale: It says the system should plan by predicting action consequences and recovering from unexpected outcomes.

r003.rationale: It mentions adding memory, a world model, and a planning mechanism, but does not suggest adding search.

r004.rationale: It does not observe that current mathematics or coding LLM systems already use search and planning.

sol-6.1.text:
I would need to see a system that can learn how an unfamiliar environment works, figure out what actions will accomplish a goal, and adapt when something unexpected happens. And do this reliably, without requiring an enormous number of examples of every situation it might encounter.

For example, give it a new task that requires a sequence of actions, where mistakes have consequences and it cannot simply try every possibility. Can it predict the consequences of its actions? Can it revise its plan when its predictions are wrong? Can it learn something from that experience and use it on the next task?

If an LLM could demonstrate those abilities robustly, I would revise my view. But we have to distinguish the language model from the entire system around it. If you add a world model, a memory, and a planning mechanism, and the resulting system succeeds, that is very interesting. The question then is which components are responsible for those capabilities.

r001.rationale: The response asks for success on a new task and robust adaptation, but does not specify zero-shot execution.

r002.rationale: It asks whether the system can predict action consequences and revise its plan when predictions are wrong.

r003.rationale: It mentions adding a world model, memory, and planning mechanism, but does not suggest augmenting the LLM with search.

r004.rationale: It makes no observation about current mathematics or coding systems using search and planning.
